chsGm.GName: Magnus v Hikaru 2020 World Championship Game 6 Grand Final

moves.Annot: White stakes an immediate claim in the center, opening lines of development for the queen and dark-squared bishop. Black prevents an immediate e2-e4 and keeps his defensive options flexible.
White broadens his spatial grip on the center and clears c3 for knight development. Black prepares classical central counterplay while keeping the door open for a Nimzo-Indian or Queen's Gambit.
Developing naturally and renewing the threat to establish full central domination with e2-e4. The hallmark of the Nimzo-Indian Defense, immediately pinning the knight to contest the vital e4-square.
The solid Rubinstein System shores up d4 and paves the way for kingside piece mobilization. Black ushers his monarch into early safety before initiating operations in the center.
The bishop assumes an aggressive post aimed directly at Black's kingside. Black immediately counterattacks the base of White's center, challenging the d4-pawn.
Developing the knight here prevents doubled pawns should Black capture on c3 and leaves the f-pawn unblocked. Black strikes boldly in the center, precipitating a full-scale pawn clash.

Carlsen immediately puts the question to the bishop, compelling Black to declare his intentions. Black cedes the bishop pair to inflict doubled pawns on White, a quintessential Nimzo-Indian transaction.
White recaptures toward the center, accepting structural asymmetries for long-term dynamic compensation. Black resolves the central tension and forces White's bishop to move a second time.
The bishop recaptures while maintaining pressure along the a2-g8 diagonal. Black lines up on the c-file against White's bishop, preparing ...b6 and ...Bb7.
Anticipating discoveries along the c-file, the bishop retreats to an ideal, secure diagonal. Black prepares to fianchetto his light-squared bishop to exert long-range pressure down the board.
White tucks his king away and readies his rooks for the central breakthrough. Black boldly pins the knight against the f1-rook, hindering White's piece coordination.
Developing the bishop on the long diagonal to support the eventual central advance. Black brings another piece into the fray, exerting pressure on the d4-square.
Stationing the rook behind the c-pawn readies the thematic c3-c4 thrust. Black logically opposes White along the semi-open c-file.
Carlsen advances his mobile pawn center, seizing space and activating his bishop on b2. Black clarifies the central tension, seeking to saddle White with vulnerable hanging pawns.
White accepts hanging pawns, obtaining dynamic central control and sweeping diagonals for both bishops. The queen vacates the c-file to link the rooks and increase pressure on a3.
A classic central breakthrough that detonates the position and unleashes White's pieces. Black must capture, as permitting the pawn to advance further would fatally suffocate his position.
Carlsen spurns an immediate recapture to seize the open e-file against Black's queen. Black snatches a pawn, hoping his active pieces can weather the impending tempest.
The knight leaps into the attack with tempo, clearing the e-file and aiming directly at the kingside. Black's queen retreats to safety, parrying immediate tactical threats.

Repositioning the bishop along the lethal b1-h7 diagonal signals an all-out assault against Black's king. Black bolsters his c4-bishop, but queenside pawn moves offer little defense against the gathering storm.
A menacing outpost that exerts suffocating pressure on g7 and invites the white queen into the attack. Black pushes his passed pawn to shut down the b2-bishop's line of fire.
The queen prepares to swing into the kingside via g5 or h6 while connecting rooks along the first rank. Black seeks to eliminate the troublesome f5-knight and relieve the defensive burden.

Carlsen lifts his rook with lethal versatility, intending to transfer it into the attack or double on the rank. Black covers the b5-pawn, but this passive gesture leaves his king bereft of reinforcements.
A magnificent piece sacrifice that demolishes the pawn shield guarding Black's king. Black has no choice but to accept, stepping into a devastating crossfire.
Delivering check with tempo and driving the monarch deeper into the corner. The only legal response, leaving Black's king completely cornered.
The queen pivots to pin the f6-knight while threatening mate, tightening the lethal noose. Black seeks counterplay along the g-file and attempts to overprotect his monarch.
A brilliant deflection sacrifice that strips away the key defender of the central d4-pawn. Black must recapture, but his pieces are now fatally uncoordinated.
The bishop recaptures with crushing force, renewing the lethal pin against the f6-knight. The king steps forward to defend the pinned knight, but walks into fresh lines of fire.
White pockets another pawn with check, thoroughly stripping Black's king of shelter. The king is forced out into the open, fleeing the lethal kingside sector.
Checking again to deny the king any respite and keep the defense off-balance. The king scurries to the center, but finds no safe haven on the open board.
White chops off the pinned knight, liquidating Black's resistance and keeping material superiority. Black counters with a queen attack against the e1-rook, but the threat is easily parried.
White defends the rook while coordinating his queen with the active bishop pair. Offering a queen trade in a desperate bid to dampen White's attacking momentum.
Carlsen decisively seizes the open d-file, creating irresistible threats of back-rank infiltration. Black interposes his rook on the d-file to prevent an immediate collapse.
The bishop retreats with tempo, hitting the queen while unmasking a battery down the d-file. The queen steps aside to keep an eye on critical central defense points.
Another piece joins the attack with tempo, driving the queen to yet another passive square. Black seeks shelter on c4, though his pieces remain hopelessly tied down.
A cool, prophylactic measure that provides the white king with luft and quells any back-rank surprises. Black attempts an escape to the queenside, but his king walks into a minefield.
A quiet, patient consolidation that prepares to double rooks or maneuver flexibly. Black pins the bishop along the e-file in search of last-ditch counterplay.
Stepping off the long diagonal to eliminate any tactical pins and safeguard the king completely. Black pins White's bishop against the queen, hoping for a tactical reprieve.
A stinging check that compels Black's bishop to retreat into another pin. Black must block, but his defensive resources are now entirely exhausted.
The bishop retreats to attack the enemy queen, relentlessly driving her away from the central action. The queen is forced to the edge of the board, leaving her king utterly defenseless.
Carlsen unmasks the d-file, weaving an inescapable web of discovered checks around the black monarch. The rook desperately interposes, but the king cannot survive the converging fire.
The crowning blow, penetrating with decisive checkmate threats and forcing Black's immediate capitulation.

chsGm.GName: King's Gambit Accepted / Bishop's Gambit / Bryan Countergambit - Adolf Anderssen vs. Lionel Kieseritzky, The Immortal Game

moves.Annot: White stakes an immediate claim in the center and frees paths for both queen and light-squared bishop. Black responds symmetrically to contest central territory and maintain parity.

The King's Gambit strikes instantly at Black's central outpost, offering a flank pawn to secure central dominance and open the f-file. Black accepts the challenge, intending to hold the extra material or exploit the weakened diagonal leading to White's king.

Anderssen initiates the Bishop's Gambit, training his sights on the delicate f7-pawn while keeping the f-file unobstructed for his rook. Kieseritzky seizes the open diagonal with an immediate check to strip White of his castling rights.

White steps aside calmly, confident that his dynamic center outweighs the displaced king. The Bryan Countergambit sacrifices a wing pawn to lure White's bishop away from its aggressive post against f7.
Anderssen accepts the gift, keeping a material balance while maintaining active piece play. Black rapidly brings out his kingside knight to attack the undefended e4-pawn and accelerate development.

A classic developing move that shields the e4-pawn while harassing Black's exposed queen. Kieseritzky tucks the queen away to keep an eye on f4, though the queen remains clumsy and prone to further tactical harassment.

Solidifying the e4-outpost while uncorking the dark-squared bishop to eye the gambit pawn. Black shifts the knight to threaten a vicious check on g3, but violates opening principles by moving the same piece twice.
White parries the fork threat by vacating f3 and targeting the critical f5-outpost. Black steps into the line of fire to simultaneously threaten White's bishop on b5 and knight on h4.

White plants the knight on an unassailable outpost, exerting immense tactical pressure on Black's kingside. Black drives the bishop away while securing a retreat square for his queen, yet compromises his queenside structure.

Rather than retreating, White launches an aggressive wing thrust that dislodges the black knight and defends the bishop tactically. Black must retreat his knight to f6, renewing an attack on the newly advanced g4-pawn.

Anderssen ignores the threat to his bishop and supports his pawn along the semi-open file, offering a piece for overwhelming initiative. Kieseritzky accepts the bishop, unaware that his queen is drifting into an inescapable web.
Advancing the pawn strips the black queen of crucial operating space and drives her backward. Black has only one viable square to keep the monarch protected and avoid outright loss of the queen.
White relentlessly pursues the queen, herding her deeper into hostile territory while gaining valuable space. Black must cling to g5, as any other retreat drops the piece immediately.

Developing the queen creates two deadly threats: discovering an attack on Black's queen with Bxf4 and unleashing e5 to fork Black's rooks. Kieseritzky is forced into a tragic retreat to g8 to manufacture an escape path for his trapped queen.

White finally recovers the gambit pawn with rapid piece development, activating his entire army against Black's sleeping forces. Black repositions the queen with tempo against the b2-pawn, desperately seeking counterplay.

Anderssen brings his final minor piece into the attack, aiming directly for the vulnerable d5 and b5 entry points. Black develops his bishop to attack the g1-rook, underestimating White's explosive attacking potential.
A devastating central leap that threatens the devastating fork on c7. Kieseritzky grabs the b2-pawn and attacks both white rooks, but material greed proves fatal against superior piece activity.

A legendary deflection offering both rooks to sever the queen's connection to the critical defense of e7 and c7. Black accepts the rook with bishop, hoping White's onslaught will stall without major pieces.

A magnificent interference sacrifice that cuts off the black queen's diagonal defense of the g7-pawn. Black captures the second rook with check, remaining completely oblivious to the mate approaching his own king.
The king calmly sidesteps the check, safe and snug while Black's rooks and queen sit stranded on the perimeter. Black belatedly mobilizes the queenside knight to control the lethal c7-mating square.
The knight rips open the king's shelter, delivering a forcing check that pulls the monarch onto the fatal d8-square. Black has no choice but to step his king aside into the tightening noose.
The immortal queen sacrifice that forcibly deflects Black's only remaining defender from the e7-square. Black is compelled to capture the queen, sealing his own execution.
Pure aesthetic perfection: three minor pieces deliver checkmate in the heart of Black's camp while all of Black's heavy artillery watches in vain.
